To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) recommended doses of phytosterols are not consumed, (2) phytosterols can modestly reduce total serum cholesterol in the community and (3) the effect of phytosterolemargarine cannot equal the effect that is seen in cholesterol-lowering drugs.
the phytosterol and phytostanols-enriched margarinesthat were introduced on the market in 1999 in the Netherlands are not consumed as recommended.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of food as a vehicle for delivering functional ingredients.
the use of phytosterols and phytostanols as cholesterol-lowering food ingredients.
the effects of phytosterols on the human body, with a particular focus on the effects of phyto- sterols on cholesterol levels in the blood.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the use of phytosterols in the form of margarine is not a substitute for the use of statins, and that it is important to educate the public about the cholesterol lowering properties of these foods and drugs.
the study shows that phytosterol-/-stanol-en riched margarine can reduce cholesterol in the community and that it cannot replace cholesterol lowering drugs, but can act additively.
the use of phytosterols in food products is an effective strategy for the prevention of cardiovascular disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of phytosterols and phytostanols in food and food supplements can be an effective strategy to lower blood cholesterol.

phytosterol or phytostanol margarines are not consumed in recommended amounts, but they can modestly reduce cholesterol in the community, and that they cannot equal the effect on cholesterol of cholesterol-lowering medication.
phytosterol or phytostanol enriched margarine can modestly reduce total serum cholesterol, but not to the extent of cholesterol-lowering medications.
The main takeaway from our work is that
phytosterol and phytostanols are safe for human use, but they are not as effective at lowering cholesterol levels as cholesterol-lowering drugs.
